Caring for someone who has Alzheimer's disease (AD) can be stressful and overwhelming. It's important to take care of yourself. Ask for and accept help. Talk to the doctor. Find out what treatments might help control symptoms or address behavior problems. Find a support group. Others who have "been there" may be able to help and will understand. If there are times of day that the person is less confused or more cooperative, take advantage of that in daily routines. Consider using adult day care or respite services. These offer a break with the peace of mind that the patient is being taken care of. Begin to plan for the future. This may include - Getting financial and legal documents in order - Looking into assisted living or nursing homes - Finding out what your health insurance and Medicare will cover NIH: National Institute on Aging

Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most common form of dementia among older people. Dementia is a brain disorder that seriously affects a person's ability to carry out daily activities. AD begins slowly. It first involves the parts of the brain that control thought, memory and language. People with AD may have trouble remembering things that happened recently or names of people they know. A related problem, mild cognitive impairment (MCI), causes more memory problems than normal for people of the same age. Many, but not all, people with MCI will develop AD. In AD, over time, symptoms get worse. People may not recognize family members. They may have trouble speaking, reading or writing. They may forget how to brush their teeth or comb their hair. Later on, they may become anxious or aggressive, or wander away from home. Eventually, they need total care. This can cause great stress for family members who must care for them. AD usually begins after age 60. The risk goes up as you get older. Your risk is also higher if a family member has had the disease. No treatment can stop the disease. However, some drugs may help keep symptoms from getting worse for a limited time. NIH: National Institute on Aging

Amblyopia, or "lazy eye," is the most common cause of visual impairment in children. It happens when an eye fails to work properly with the brain. The eye may look normal, but the brain favors the other eye. In some cases, it can affect both eyes. Causes include - Strabismus - a disorder in which the two eyes don't line up in the same direction - Refractive error in an eye - when one eye cannot focus as well as the other, because of a problem with its shape. This includes nearsightedness, farsightedness, and astigmatism. - Cataract - a clouding in the lens of the eye It can be hard to diagnose amblyopia. It is often found during a routine vision exam. Treatment for amblyopia forces the child to use the eye with weaker vision. There are two common ways to do this. One is to have the child wear a patch over the good eye for several hours each day, over a number of weeks to months. The other is with eye drops that temporarily blur vision. Each day, the child gets a drop of a drug called atropine in the stronger eye. It is also sometimes necessary to treat the underlying cause. This could include glasses or surgery. NIH: National Eye Institute

Amyloidosis occurs when abnormal proteins called amyloids build up and form deposits. The deposits can collect in organs such as the kidney and heart. This can cause the organs to become stiff and unable to work the way they should. There are three main types of amyloidosis: - Primary - with no known cause - Secondary - caused by another disease, including some types of cancer - Familial - passed down through genes Symptoms can vary, depending upon which organs are affected. Treatment depends on the type of amyloidosis you have. The goal is to help with symptoms and limit the production of proteins. If another disease is the cause, it needs to be treated.

Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a nervous system disease that attacks nerve cells called neurons in your brain and spinal cord. These neurons transmit messages from your brain and spinal cord to your voluntary muscles - the ones you can control, like in your arms and legs. At first, this causes mild muscle problems. Some people notice - Trouble walking or running - Trouble writing - Speech problems Eventually, you lose your strength and cannot move. When muscles in your chest fail, you cannot breathe. A breathing machine can help, but most people with ALS die from respiratory failure. The disease usually strikes between age 40 and 60. More men than women get it. No one knows what causes ALS. It can run in families, but usually it strikes at random. There is no cure. Medicines can relieve symptoms and, sometimes, prolong survival. NIH: National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke

Summary : Anabolic steroids are man-made substances related to male sex hormones. Doctors use anabolic steroids to treat some hormone problems in men, delayed puberty, and muscle loss from some diseases. Bodybuilders and athletes often use anabolic steroids to build muscles and improve athletic performance. Using them this way is not legal or safe. Abuse of anabolic steroids has been linked with many health problems. They include - Acne - Breast growth and shrinking of testicles in men - Voice deepening and growth of facial hair in women - High blood pressure - Heart problems, including heart attack - Liver disease, including cancer - Kidney damage - Aggressive behavior NIH: National Institute on Drug Abuse

The anus is where stool leaves your body when you go to the bathroom. It is made up of your outer layers of skin and the end of your large intestine. Anal cancer is a disease in which cancer cells form in the tissues of the anus. Anal cancer is rare. It is more common in smokers and people over 50. You are also at higher risk if you have HPV, have anal sex, or have many sexual partners. Symptoms include bleeding, pain, or lumps in the anal area. Anal itching and discharge can also be signs of anal cancer. Doctors use tests that examine the anus to diagnose anal cancer. They include a physical exam, endoscopy, ultrasound, and biopsy. Treatments include radiation therapy, chemotherapy, and surgery. NIH: National Cancer Institute

The anus is the opening of the rectum through which stool passes out of your body. Problems with the anus are common. They include hemorrhoids, abscesses, fissures (cracks), and cancer. You may be embarrassed to talk about your anal troubles. But it is important to let your doctor know, especially if you have pain or bleeding. The more details you can give about your problem, the better your doctor will be able to help you. Treatments vary depending on the particular problem. NIH: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases

Anaphylaxis is a serious allergic reaction. It can begin very quickly, and symptoms may be life-threatening. The most common causes are reactions to foods (especially peanuts), medications, and stinging insects. Other causes include exercise and exposure to latex. Sometimes no cause can be found. It can affect many organs: - Skin - itching, hives, redness, swelling - Nose - sneezing, stuffy nose, runny nose - Mouth - itching, swelling of the lips or tongue - Throat - itching, tightness, trouble swallowing, swelling of the back of the throat - Chest - shortness of breath, coughing, wheezing, chest pain or tightness - Heart - weak pulse, passing out, shock - Gastrointestinal tract - vomiting, diarrhea, cramps - Nervous system - dizziness or fainting If someone is having a serious allergic reaction, call 9-1-1. If an auto-injector is available, give the person the injection right away. NIH: National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases
Summary : Anatomy is the science that studies the structure of the body. On this page, you'll find links to descriptions and pictures of the human body's parts and organ systems from head to toe.

If you have anemia, your blood does not carry enough oxygen to the rest of your body. The most common cause of anemia is not having enough iron. Your body needs iron to make hemoglobin. Hemoglobin is an iron-rich protein that gives the red color to blood. It carries oxygen from the lungs to the rest of the body. Anemia has three main causes: blood loss, lack of red blood cell production, and high rates of red blood cell destruction. Conditions that may lead to anemia include - Heavy periods - Pregnancy - Ulcers - Colon polyps or colon cancer - Inherited disorders - A diet that does not have enough iron, folic acid or vitamin B12 - Blood disorders such as sickle cell anemia and thalassemia, or cancer - Aplastic anemia, a condition that can be inherited or acquired - G6PD deficiency, a metabolic disorder Anemia can make you feel tired, cold, dizzy, and irritable. You may be short of breath or have a headache. Your doctor will diagnose anemia with a physical exam and blood tests. Treatment depends on the kind of anemia you have. NIH: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute

If you are having surgery, your doctor will give you medicine called an anesthetic. Anesthetics reduce or prevent pain. There are three main types: - Local - numbs one small area of the body. You stay awake and alert. - Regional - blocks pain in an area of the body, such an arm or leg. A common type is epidural anesthesia, which is often used during childbirth. - General - makes you unconscious. You do not feel any pain, and you do not remember the procedure afterwards. You may also get a mild sedative to relax you. You stay awake but may not remember the procedure afterwards. Sedation can be used with or without anesthesia. The type of anesthesia or sedation you get depends on many factors. They include the procedure you are having and your current health.

An aneurysm is a bulge or "ballooning" in the wall of an artery. Arteries are blood vessels that carry oxygen-rich blood from the heart to other parts of the body. If an aneurysm grows large, it can burst and cause dangerous bleeding or even death. Most aneurysms occur in the aorta, the main artery that runs from the heart through the chest and abdomen. Aneurysms also can happen in arteries in the brain, heart and other parts of the body. If an aneurysm in the brain bursts, it causes a stroke. Aneurysms can develop and become large before causing any symptoms. Often doctors can stop aneurysms from bursting if they find and treat them early. They use imaging tests to find aneurysms. Often aneurysms are found by chance during tests done for other reasons. Medicines and surgery are the two main treatments for aneurysms. NIH: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute

Angina is chest pain or discomfort you feel when there is not enough blood flow to your heart muscle. Your heart muscle needs the oxygen that the blood carries. Angina may feel like pressure or a squeezing pain in your chest. It may feel like indigestion. You may also feel pain in your shoulders, arms, neck, jaw, or back. Angina is a symptom of coronary artery disease (CAD), the most common heart disease. CAD happens when a sticky substance called plaque builds up in the arteries that supply blood to the heart, reducing blood flow. There are three types of angina: - Stable angina is the most common type. It happens when the heart is working harder than usual. Stable angina has a regular pattern. Rest and medicines usually help. - Unstable angina is the most dangerous. It does not follow a pattern and can happen without physical exertion. It does not go away with rest or medicine. It is a sign that you could have a heart attack soon. - Variant angina is rare. It happens when you are resting. Medicines can help. Not all chest pain or discomfort is angina. If you have chest pain, you should see your health care provider. NIH: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute

Summary : If you have coronary artery disease, the arteries in your heart are narrowed or blocked by a sticky material called plaque. Angioplasty is a procedure to restore blood flow through the artery. You have angioplasty in a hospital. The doctor threads a thin tube through a blood vessel in the arm or groin up to the involved site in the artery. The tube has a tiny balloon on the end. When the tube is in place, the doctor inflates the balloon to push the plaque outward against the wall of the artery. This widens the artery and restores blood flow. Doctors may use angioplasty to - Reduce chest pain caused by reduced blood flow to the heart - Minimize damage to heart muscle from a heart attack Many people go home the day after angioplasty, and are able to return to work within a week of coming home. NIH: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute

Wild animals usually avoid people. They might attack, however, if they feel threatened, are sick, or are protecting their young or territory. Attacks by pets are more common. Animal bites rarely are life-threatening, but if they become infected, you can develop serious medical problems. To prevent animal bites and complications from bites - Never pet, handle, or feed unknown animals - Leave snakes alone - Watch your children closely around animals - Vaccinate your cats, ferrets, and dogs against rabies - Spay or neuter your dog to make it less aggressive - Get a tetanus booster if you have not had one recently - Wear boots and long pants when you are in areas with venomous snakes If an animal bites you, clean the wound with soap and water as soon as possible. Get medical attention if necessary. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

Animal diseases that people can catch are called zoonoses. Many diseases affecting humans can be traced to animals or animal products. You can get a disease directly from an animal, or indirectly, through the environment. Farm animals can carry diseases. If you touch them or things they have touched, like fencing or buckets, wash your hands thoroughly. Adults should make sure children who visit farms or petting zoos wash up as well. Though they may be cute and cuddly, wild animals may carry germs, viruses, and parasites. Deer and deer mice carry ticks that cause Lyme disease. Some wild animals may carry rabies. Enjoy wildlife from a distance. Pets can also make you sick. Reptiles pose a particular risk. Turtles, snakes and iguanas can transmit Salmonella bacteria to their owners. You can get rabies from an infected dog or toxoplasmosis from handling kitty litter of an infected cat. The chance that your dog or cat will make you sick is small. You can reduce the risk by practicing good hygiene, keeping pet areas clean and keeping your pets' shots up-to-date.

Your ankle bone and the ends of your two lower leg bones make up the ankle joint. Your ligaments, which connect bones to one another, stabilize and support it. Your muscles and tendons move it. The most common ankle problems are sprains and fractures. A sprain is an injury to the ligaments. It may take a few weeks to many months to heal completely. A fracture is a break in a bone. You can also injure other parts of the ankle such as tendons, which join muscles to bone, and cartilage, which cushions your joints. Ankle sprains and fractures are common sports injuries.

Ankylosing spondylitis is a type of arthritis of the spine. It causes inflammation between your vertebrae, which are the bones that make up your spine, and in the joints between your spine and pelvis. In some people, it can affect other joints. AS is more common and more severe in men. It often runs in families. The cause is unknown, but it is likely that both genes and factors in the environment play a role. Early symptoms of AS include back pain and stiffness. These problems often start in late adolescence or early adulthood. Over time, AS can fuse your vertebrae together, limiting movement. Some people have symptoms that come and go. Others have severe, ongoing pain. A diagnosis of AS is based on your medical history and a physical examination. You may also have imaging or blood tests. AS has no cure, but medicines can relieve symptoms and may keep the disease from getting worse. Eating a healthy diet, not smoking, and exercising can also help. In rare cases, you may need surgery to straighten the spine. NIH: National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Disease

Anthrax is a disease caused by Bacillus anthracis, a germ that lives in soil. Many people know about it from the 2001 bioterror attacks. In the attacks, someone purposely spread anthrax through the U.S. mail. This killed five people and made 22 sick. Anthrax is rare. It affects animals such as cattle, sheep, and goats more often than people. People can get anthrax from contact with infected animals, wool, meat, or hides. It can cause three forms of disease in people. They are - Cutaneous, which affects the skin. People with cuts or open sores can get it if they touch the bacteria. - Inhalation, which affects the lungs. You can get this if you breathe in spores of the bacteria. - Gastrointestinal, which affects the digestive system. You can get it by eating infected meat. Antibiotics often cure anthrax if it is diagnosed early. But many people don't know they have anthrax until it is too late to treat. A vaccine to prevent anthrax is available for people in the military and others at high risk. NIH: National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases

Summary : Antibiotics are medicines that fight bacterial infections. Used properly, they can save lives. But there is a growing problem of antibiotic resistance. It happens when bacteria change and become able to resist the effects of an antibiotic. Using antibiotics can lead to resistance. Each time you take antibiotics, sensitive bacteria are killed. But resistant germs may be left to grow and multiply. They can spread to other people. They can also cause infections that certain antibiotics cannot cure. Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) is one example. It causes infections that are resistant to several common antibiotics. To help prevent antibiotic resistance - Don't use antibiotics for viruses like colds or flu. Antibiotics don't work on viruses. - Don't pressure your doctor to give you an antibiotic. - When you take antibiotics, follow the directions carefully. Finish your medicine even if you feel better. If you stop treatment too soon, some bacteria may survive and re-infect you. - Don't save antibiotics for later or use someone else's prescription. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

Summary : Antibiotics are powerful medicines that fight bacterial infections. Used properly, antibiotics can save lives. They either kill bacteria or keep them from reproducing. Your body's natural defenses can usually take it from there. Antibiotics do not fight infections caused by viruses, such as - Colds - Flu - Most coughs and bronchitis - Sore throats, unless caused by strep If a virus is making you sick, taking antibiotics may do more harm than good. Using antibiotics when you don't need them, or not using them properly, can add to antibiotic resistance. This happens when bacteria change and become able to resist the effects of an antibiotic. When you take antibiotics, follow the directions carefully. It is important to finish your medicine even if you feel better. If you stop treatment too soon, some bacteria may survive and re-infect you. Do not save antibiotics for later or use someone else's prescription. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

Summary : Antidepressants are medicines that treat depression. Your doctor can prescribe them for you. They work to balance some of the natural chemicals in our brains. It may take several weeks for them to help. There are several types of antidepressants. You and your doctor may have to try a few before finding what works best for you. Antidepressants may cause mild side effects that usually do not last long. These may include headache, nausea, sleep problems, restlessness, and sexual problems. Tell your doctor if you have any side effects. You should also let your doctor know if you take any other medicines, vitamins, or herbal supplements. It is important to keep taking your medicines, even if you feel better. Do not stop taking your medicines without talking to your doctor. You often need to stop antidepressants gradually. NIH: National Institute of Mental Health

Summary : Antioxidants are man-made or natural substances that may prevent or delay some types of cell damage. Antioxidants are found in many foods, including fruits and vegetables. They are also available as dietary supplements. Examples of antioxidants include - Beta-carotene - Lutein - Lycopene - Selenium - Vitamin A - Vitamin C - Vitamin E Vegetables and fruits are rich sources of antioxidants. There is good evidence that eating a diet with lots of vegetables and fruits is healthy and lowers risks of certain diseases. But it isn't clear whether this is because of the antioxidants, something else in the foods, or other factors. High-dose supplements of antioxidants may be linked to health risks in some cases. For example, high doses of beta-carotene may increase the risk of lung cancer in smokers. High doses of vitamin E may increase risks of prostate cancer and one type of stroke. Antioxidant supplements may also interact with some medicines. To minimize risk, tell you of your health care providers about any antioxidants you use. NIH: National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health

Fear and anxiety are part of life. You may feel anxious before you take a test or walk down a dark street. This kind of anxiety is useful - it can make you more alert or careful. It usually ends soon after you are out of the situation that caused it. But for millions of people in the United States, the anxiety does not go away, and gets worse over time. They may have chest pains or nightmares. They may even be afraid to leave home. These people have anxiety disorders. Types include - Panic disorder - Obsessive-compulsive disorder - Post-traumatic stress disorder - Phobias - Generalized anxiety disorder Treatment can involve medicines, therapy or both. NIH: National Institute of Mental Health

An aneurysm is a bulge or "ballooning" in the wall of an artery. Arteries are blood vessels that carry oxygen-rich blood from the heart to other parts of the body. If an aneurysm grows large, it can burst and cause dangerous bleeding or even death. Most aneurysms are in the aorta, the main artery that runs from the heart through the chest and abdomen. There are two types of aortic aneurysm: - Thoracic aortic aneurysms - these occur in the part of the aorta running through the chest - Abdominal aortic aneurysms - these occur in the part of the aorta running through the abdomen Most aneurysms are found during tests done for other reasons. Some people are at high risk for aneurysms. It is important for them to get screening, because aneurysms can develop and become large before causing any symptoms Screening is recommended for people between the ages of 65 and 75 if they have a family history, or if they are men who have smoked. Doctors use imaging tests to find aneurysms. Medicines and surgery are the two main treatments. NIH: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute

Aphasia is a disorder caused by damage to the parts of the brain that control language. It can make it hard for you to read, write, and say what you mean to say. It is most common in adults who have had a stroke. Brain tumors, infections, injuries, and dementia can also cause it. The type of problem you have and how bad it is depends on which part of your brain is damaged and how much damage there is. There are four main types: - Expressive aphasia - you know what you want to say, but you have trouble saying or writing what you mean - Receptive aphasia - you hear the voice or see the print, but you can't make sense of the words - Anomic aphasia - you have trouble using the correct word for objects, places, or events - Global aphasia - you can't speak, understand speech, read, or write Some people recover from aphasia without treatment. Most, however, need language therapy as soon as possible. NIH: National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke

answers_clean:
A1C (also known as hemoglobin A1c) is a blood test that provides an average of your blood sugar levels over the past 2 to 3 months. It's used primarily to diagnose prediabetes and diabetes and to monitor how well blood sugars are being controlled in those with diagnosed diabetes.

The results are given as a percentage; for example:
- Normal range: Below 5.7%
- Prediabetes: Between 5.7% - 6.4%
- Diabetes: 6.5% or higher

For people managing diabetes, healthcare providers often recommend maintaining an A1C level below 7%, but this target can vary depending on individual health circumstances. Regular testing helps guide treatment decisions and lifestyle adjustments aimed at preventing complications from high blood glucose levels.

Abdominal pain refers to discomfort or pain felt in the belly area between the chest and groin. It can vary widely in severity and may be caused by various conditions such as indigestion, gas, constipation, infection, inflammation, injury, or more serious disorders like appendicitis, ulcers, irritable bowel syndrome, or tumors. The type of treatment depends on identifying the underlying cause.

Abortion refers to the termination of pregnancy before the fetus can survive outside the womb, resulting in the expulsion or extraction of an embryo or fetus. It can occur spontaneously as a miscarriage or be induced medically or surgically for various reasons including health concerns, personal choice, or fetal abnormalities.

An abscess is a localized collection of pus caused by infection, typically surrounded by swollen tissue. It forms as part of the body's defense mechanism to contain infections. Common causes include bacterial infections; they can occur in various parts of the body including skin, teeth, or internal organs. Symptoms often include pain, swelling, redness, and warmth at the site. Treatment usually involves antibiotics and sometimes drainage of the pus.

Acne is a common skin condition characterized by pimples, blackheads, whiteheads, and cysts that occur when hair follicles become clogged with oil and dead skin cells. It typically affects areas of the body with high numbers of sebaceous glands such as the face, back, chest, shoulders, and neck. Hormonal changes often trigger acne development due to increased production of oils in the skin.

An acoustic neuroma, also known as vestibular schwannoma, is a benign tumor that develops on the eighth cranial nerve leading from the inner ear to the brain. This nerve plays a crucial role in hearing and balance; therefore, symptoms often include gradual hearing loss, tinnitus (ringing in the ears), dizziness or vertigo, and sometimes facial numbness if the tumor grows large enough to press against nearby nerves. Treatment options vary depending on factors such as size of the tumor, patient's age, overall health status, and severity of symptoms, including monitoring with regular MRI scans for small tumors without significant growth, radiation therapy, or surgical removal.

Acupuncture is an ancient form of Chinese medicine involving the insertion of thin needles into specific points (acupoints) on the body to balance energy flow or "Qi." It aims to treat various conditions such as pain management, stress relief, nausea, migraines, and more by stimulating nerve endings and muscles. The practice is generally considered safe when performed by licensed practitioners using sterile equipment. Scientific research supports its effectiveness for certain ailments but varies across different health issues. Always consult with healthcare providers before starting acupuncture treatment.

Acute bronchitis is an inflammation of the lining of the bronchial tubes, which carry air to and from your lungs. It's often caused by viral infections such as those that cause colds or flu, though it can also be triggered by bacterial infection or exposure to irritants like tobacco smoke or pollutants. Symptoms typically include coughing up mucus, shortness of breath, chest discomfort, fatigue, sore throat, mild fever, and body aches. Most cases resolve within two weeks without specific treatment beyond symptom management.

Acute lymphocytic leukemia (ALL), also known as acute lymphoblastic leukemia, is a type of cancer that affects blood-forming cells in the bone marrow, specifically involving white blood cells called lymphocytes. It progresses rapidly without treatment and leads to an overproduction of immature lymphocytes (lymphoblasts). These abnormal cells crowd out healthy blood cells, impairing normal immune function and other bodily processes dependent on proper blood cell activity. ALL is most common in children but can occur at any age. Treatment typically involves chemotherapy aimed at destroying these malignant cells.

Addison's disease, also known as primary adrenal insufficiency, is a rare disorder where the adrenal glands don't produce enough of certain hormones, primarily cortisol and often aldosterone. It results from damage to the outer layer (cortex) of the adrenal glands, usually due to an autoimmune response but can also be caused by infections or other diseases affecting these glands. Symptoms include fatigue, muscle weakness, weight loss, low blood pressure, and hyperpigmentation. Treatment typically involves hormone replacement therapy.

Adhesions are bands of scar tissue that form between tissues and organs, causing them to stick together abnormally. They can develop in any part of the body but commonly occur in the abdomen or pelvis after surgery or inflammation such as from infections like appendicitis. Adhesions may cause pain and complications including bowel obstruction.

Adoption is a legal process where an individual or couple becomes the lawful parent(s) of a child who was not born to them. This can involve several types:

1. Domestic adoption - Adopting within one's own country.
2. International adoption - Adopting from another country.
3. Foster care adoption - Taking in children through foster care systems with the goal of adopting.
4. Stepparent adoption - When a stepparent legally adopts their spouse’s biological child.

The process typically includes background checks, home studies by social workers, and court proceedings to finalize the adoption order. Requirements vary significantly between jurisdictions regarding eligibility criteria for adoptive parents as well as procedures involved throughout the process.

Adrenal gland cancer refers to malignant tumors that develop in one or both of the adrenal glands, which sit atop each kidney. The most common type is adrenocortical carcinoma, originating from the outer layer (cortex). Symptoms can include unexplained weight loss, abdominal pain, feeling full quickly when eating, and symptoms related to excess hormone production like hypertension for cortisol-producing tumors or sexual characteristic changes for aldosterone- or sex-hormone producing ones. Treatment often involves surgery followed by chemotherapy or radiation therapy depending on the stage and specifics of the tumor.

Adrenal gland disorders involve conditions affecting the adrenal glands' function or structure, which can lead to hormone production imbalances. Common types include:

1. **Cushing's Syndrome**: Caused by excessive cortisol levels due to prolonged exposure to high corticosteroid levels from either an external source like medication or internal causes such as tumors.

2. **Addison’s Disease (Primary Adrenocortical Insufficiency)**: Occurs when the adrenal cortex does not produce enough of certain hormones, particularly cortisol and aldosterone, often resulting from autoimmune destruction but also possibly caused by infections or other diseases that damage the adrenal glands.

3. **Conn's Syndrome (Primary Aldosteronism)**: Characterized by overproduction of aldosterone leading to hypertension and hypokalemia (low potassium).

4. **Pheochromocytoma**: A rare tumor usually found in one of your adrenal glands that secretes excess epinephrine and norepinephrine causing symptoms including severe headaches, palpitations, sweating, anxiety, tremor, pallor, nausea/vomiting, weight loss despite increased appetite, and hypertension.

Each disorder requires specific diagnostic tests for confirmation and tailored treatment approaches depending upon its underlying cause and severity.

An advance directive is a legal document in which a person specifies what actions should be taken for their health if they are no longer able to make decisions due to illness or incapacity. There are two main types of advance directives:

1. Living Will - A written document that outlines specific healthcare preferences and instructions.

2. Durable Power of Attorney for Healthcare (DPAHC) or Health Care Proxy - This allows an individual to appoint someone else as a proxy to make healthcare decisions when incapacitated.

Advance directives vary by state; it's important to ensure compliance with local laws regarding forms and witnessing requirements. They help clarify patient wishes, reducing stress for family members during critical times.

African Americans face unique health challenges compared to other racial groups in the United States due to various factors including socioeconomic status, access to healthcare, genetic predispositions, and environmental conditions. Some key points include:

1. **Higher Incidence of Certain Diseases**: African Americans experience higher rates of hypertension (high blood pressure), diabetes, heart disease, stroke, and certain cancers such as breast cancer among women.

2. **Health Disparities**: There is evidence of disparities in treatment outcomes for many diseases affecting this population group, often linked with systemic barriers like lack of insurance or living in areas without adequate healthcare facilities ("healthcare deserts").

3. **Genetic Factors**: Specific genetic markers can influence susceptibility to some illnesses; for example, sickle cell anemia occurs more frequently within populations originating from regions where malaria was historically prevalent.

4. **Social Determinants**: Economic instability, educational opportunities, housing quality, and community safety significantly impact overall health statuses.

5. **Mental Health Issues**: Stigma around mental illness combined with historical trauma contributes to underreporting and undertreatment of depression, anxiety disorders, etc., amongst African Americans.

Addressing these issues requires comprehensive strategies that consider both individual behaviors and broader societal changes aimed at reducing inequity across all aspects influencing public health.

"After surgery," also known as postoperative or postsurgical period, refers to the time immediately following an operation until recovery is complete. This phase involves monitoring for complications, managing pain, initiating rehabilitation if necessary, and ensuring proper wound healing. The duration of this period varies depending on the type of surgery performed and individual patient factors.

Air pollution refers to the presence of harmful substances in the air that can cause health issues or damage the environment. It includes particulate matter (PM), nitrogen dioxide (NO2), sulfur dioxide (SO2), carbon monoxide (CO), ozone (O3), and volatile organic compounds (VOCs). These pollutants come from various sources such as vehicle emissions, industrial processes, burning fossil fuels for energy production, wildfires, and agricultural activities.

Exposure to polluted air is linked with respiratory problems like asthma attacks, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) exacerbations, lung cancer, heart diseases including stroke and cardiovascular mortality, and other adverse effects on human health. Vulnerable populations include children, elderly individuals, those already suffering from respiratory conditions, and people living near high-pollution areas. Alcohol is a depressant that affects the central nervous system. It's commonly consumed in beverages like beer, wine, or spirits. Effects can include relaxation, reduced inhibitions, impaired judgment, coordination issues, and memory lapses. Long-term heavy use may lead to alcohol dependence, liver disease, heart problems, and various cancers. Moderate consumption varies by country but often refers to up to one drink per day for women and two drinks per day for men. Excessive drinking increases health risks significantly. Always consume responsibly.

Alcoholism, also known as alcohol use disorder (AUD), refers to problematic patterns of drinking that lead to health issues or impairment in daily functioning. It involves compulsive consumption despite negative consequences.

Alcohol abuse specifically denotes excessive drinking without meeting all criteria for full-blown dependence but still causing significant problems such as failure to fulfill responsibilities at work, school, home; risky behaviors while intoxicated; legal troubles due to alcohol-related incidents; continued drinking despite social/interpersonal difficulties caused by its effects. Both conditions can range from mild to severe and often require professional intervention including therapy and support groups like AA.

An allergy is an immune system reaction to a substance that is normally harmless, such as pollen, pet dander, or certain foods. When exposed to these allergens, the body mistakenly identifies them as harmful invaders and produces antibodies called Immunoglobulin E (IgE). This triggers symptoms ranging from mild (like sneezing or itching) to severe (such as anaphylaxis), depending on the individual's sensitivity and type of exposure.

Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency is a genetic disorder where the body does not produce enough of a protein called alpha-1 antitrypsin, which protects the lungs from inflammation caused by infections or inhaled irritants like tobacco smoke. This can lead to conditions such as emphysema and liver disease due to insufficient protection against tissue destruction.

Alzheimer's caregivers are individuals who provide support to people with Alzheimer’s disease or other forms of dementia. This can include family members, friends, or professional healthcare providers who assist in managing daily activities, ensuring safety, providing emotional support, coordinating medical care, and handling behavioral symptoms associated with the condition.

Alzheimer's disease is a progressive neurological disorder that leads to memory loss, cognitive decline, and behavioral changes. It is characterized by the accumulation of amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles in the brain, leading to neuronal death primarily affecting areas responsible for memory and cognition.

Amblyopia, commonly known as "lazy eye," is a condition where vision in one or both eyes does not develop properly during childhood. It results from conditions such as strabismus (misaligned eyes), significant differences in refractive error between the two eyes, or cloudiness in the eye's lens. If left untreated, amblyopia can lead to permanent visual impairment in the affected eye. Early detection and treatment, often involving patching the stronger eye or using atropine drops, can improve outcomes.

Amyloidosis is a group of rare diseases characterized by the buildup of abnormal proteins called amyloids in tissues or organs. These protein deposits can disrupt normal organ function, leading to various symptoms depending on which part of the body is affected. Commonly involved areas include the heart, kidneys, liver, spleen, nervous system, and gastrointestinal tract. Treatment often focuses on managing underlying conditions and alleviating symptoms.

Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS), also known as Lou Gehrig's disease, is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder that affects nerve cells in the brain and spinal cord leading to muscle weakness and atrophy. It impacts motor neurons responsible for voluntary movement, causing them to degenerate and die over time, which results in loss of muscle control and eventually paralysis. ALS does not affect cognitive functions or sensory capabilities like sight, touch, hearing, or taste. The exact cause remains unknown but involves complex interactions between genetics and environmental factors. Symptoms typically start with subtle difficulties such as slurred speech or limb stiffness before progressing more noticeably. There is no cure; treatment focuses on managing symptoms and slowing progression where possible.

Anabolic steroids are synthetic versions of male sex hormone testosterone used to increase muscle mass and strength. They work by stimulating protein synthesis in cells, leading to increased muscle growth when combined with exercise. Commonly abused for performance enhancement in sports despite legal restrictions and health risks including cardiovascular issues, liver damage, hormonal imbalances, and behavioral changes like aggression or depression. Medical use is limited due to these side effects but can include treating delayed puberty, some types of anemia, and recovery from injuries or surgery. Always consult healthcare providers before using any form of steroid therapy.

Anal cancer is a type of malignant tumor that forms in the tissues of the anus. It can develop from cells within the anal canal, including squamous cells, glandular cells, or immune system cells. Symptoms may include bleeding, pain, itching, or a lump near the anus. Risk factors involve HPV infection, smoking, HIV/AIDS, and chronic local inflammation. Treatment options depend on the stage but commonly include surgery, radiation therapy, chemotherapy, or a combination thereof. Early detection improves prognosis significantly.

Anal disorders refer to various conditions affecting the anus that can cause discomfort or pain. Common anal disorders include hemorrhoids, fissures, fistulas, abscesses, and incontinence. Each condition has distinct symptoms and requires specific treatment approaches. Hemorrhoids involve swollen veins around the anus; fissures are small tears; fistulas are abnormal connections between organs; abscesses are pus-filled pockets of infection; and incontinence involves an inability to control bowel movements.

Anaphylaxis is a severe, potentially life-threatening allergic reaction that can occur rapidly after exposure to an allergen such as certain foods, medications, insect stings, or latex. Symptoms may include rash, swelling of lips/tongue/face/throat, difficulty breathing, abdominal pain, vomiting/diarrhea, dizziness/fainting, rapid heartbeat, and loss of consciousness. Immediate treatment with epinephrine is critical in managing this condition.

Anatomy is the branch of science concerned with the bodily structure of humans, animals, and other living organisms. It involves the identification and understanding of organs, tissues, cells, and body parts' relationships to one another.

In human anatomy specifically:
- The skeletal system provides support and protection for softer tissues and organs; it includes 206 bones in adults.
- The muscular system consists of over 600 muscles that facilitate movement through contraction.
- The cardiovascular system comprises the heart, blood vessels (arteries, veins), and blood which circulates nutrients and oxygen throughout the body while removing waste products like carbon dioxide.
- The respiratory system allows gas exchange between the external environment and the bloodstream via lungs.
- The digestive system processes food into energy and essential nutrients using mouth, esophagus, stomach, intestines, etc.
- The nervous system coordinates actions by transmitting signals from brain and spinal cord to various body regions.
- Other systems include endocrine, urinary, reproductive, lymphatic/immune, integumentary (skin), sensory organs/systems.

Each part plays crucial roles contributing collectively towards maintaining life functions.

Anemia is a condition characterized by a deficiency of red blood cells or hemoglobin in the blood, leading to impaired oxygen delivery to body tissues. It can result from various causes including iron deficiency, vitamin deficiencies (such as B12 or folate), chronic diseases, genetic disorders like sickle cell anemia, or bone marrow problems. Symptoms often include fatigue, weakness, pale skin, shortness of breath, irregular heartbeat, dizziness, cold hands and feet, and chest pain. Treatment depends on the underlying cause but may involve dietary changes, supplements, medications, or procedures such as blood transfusions.

Anesthesia refers to medications or techniques that cause a loss of sensation, typically used to prevent pain during surgery or other medical procedures. It can be classified into general anesthesia (inducing unconsciousness), regional anesthesia (numbing a part of the body), and local anesthesia (affecting a small specific area).

Aneurysms are localized, balloon-like expansions or bulges that occur in blood vessels due to weakness in the vessel wall. They can develop anywhere but commonly affect arteries such as those found in the brain (cerebral aneurysm), abdomen (abdominal aortic aneurysm), chest (thoracic aortic aneurysm), and peripheral arteries. Rupture of an aneurysm can lead to severe internal bleeding which may be life-threatening.

Angina is chest pain or discomfort that occurs when the heart muscle does not receive enough oxygen-rich blood, often due to coronary artery disease. It's typically described as squeezing, pressure, tightness, or pain in the chest but can also affect other areas like the shoulders, arms, neck, jaw, or back. There are different types of angina including stable, unstable, variant (Prinzmetal’s), and microvascular. Management includes medications, lifestyle changes, and sometimes procedures such as angioplasty or bypass surgery depending on severity and underlying cause.

Angioplasty is a procedure used to open narrowed or blocked arteries, typically caused by atherosclerosis (plaque buildup). It involves inserting a catheter with an inflatable balloon at its tip into the affected artery, usually accessed through the groin or arm. The balloon is inflated at the site of narrowing to compress plaque against the arterial wall, thereby widening the blood vessel and improving blood flow.

Often, a stent—a small mesh tube—is placed in the artery during angioplasty to keep it propped open long-term. This helps prevent restenosis (re-narrowing) of the artery after the procedure. Commonly performed for conditions like coronary artery disease, peripheral vascular disease, and carotid artery disease, angioplasty can significantly reduce symptoms such as chest pain and improve quality of life without requiring major surgery. Recovery time varies but patients often leave the hospital within 24 hours if there are no complications.

Animal bites occur when an animal's teeth break or puncture human skin, potentially causing injury and infection. They can come from various animals such as dogs, cats, rodents, or wild animals and require proper cleaning and sometimes medical treatment to prevent complications like infections.

Animal diseases that can be transmitted to humans are known as zoonotic diseases or zoonoses. Examples include rabies from infected animals' bites, Lyme disease through tick bites, and salmonellosis via contaminated food products or contact with infected pets like reptiles and amphibians. These diseases pose risks to human health depending on exposure and preventive measures taken. Proper hygiene practices, vaccinations when available, and avoiding high-risk behaviors such as handling wild animals help in preventing transmission of these illnesses.

Ankle injuries and disorders refer to conditions affecting the ankle joint, which connects the leg bones with the foot. Common types include sprains (ligament damage), strains (muscle or tendon injury), fractures (broken bone), arthritis (joint inflammation), tendinitis (tendon inflammation), and bursitis (inflammation of fluid-filled sacs). Symptoms often involve pain, swelling, bruising, stiffness, and limited mobility in the affected area. Treatment varies depending on severity but may include rest, ice, compression, elevation, medication for pain relief, physical therapy, immobilization devices like braces or casts, and sometimes surgery.

Ankylosing Spondylitis is a type of arthritis that primarily affects the spine, causing inflammation of the spinal joints which can lead to severe pain and stiffness in the back, neck, and sometimes other joint areas. Over time, this condition may result in some degree of fusion or ankylosis where vertebrae grow together, limiting flexibility and mobility. It's part of a group of conditions known as spondyloarthropathies and typically starts in late adolescence or early adulthood.

Anthrax is an infectious disease caused by the bacterium Bacillus anthracis. It can affect both humans and animals and typically enters the body through cuts in the skin, inhalation, or ingestion. Symptoms vary depending on the route of infection but may include skin ulcers, fever, shortness of breath, nausea, and diarrhea. Treatment usually involves antibiotics and sometimes hospitalization for supportive care. Prevention includes vaccination for those at high risk such as veterinarians and livestock handlers.

Antibiotic resistance occurs when bacteria evolve mechanisms to withstand antibiotics designed to kill them or inhibit their growth. This can happen through genetic mutations or by acquiring resistant genes from other organisms. Overuse and misuse of antibiotics contribute significantly to this problem, leading to infections that are harder to treat and potentially more severe. Public health strategies focus on prudent antibiotic use, infection prevention, surveillance, and research into new antimicrobial agents.

Antibiotics are medications used to treat bacterial infections by killing or inhibiting the growth of bacteria. They do not work against viral infections such as colds or flu. Common types include penicillins (like amoxicillin), cephalosporins, macrolides (such as azithromycin), quinolones (e.g., ciprofloxacin) and tetracyclines. Proper use is crucial to prevent antibiotic resistance. Always follow healthcare provider instructions for dosage and duration when prescribed antibiotics.

Antioxidants are molecules that help prevent or slow damage to cells caused by free radicals—unstable atoms that can start harmful chain reactions in your body. Free radical formation is linked with aging as well as diseases like cancer, heart disease, diabetes, Alzheimer's, Parkinson’s, and others.

Common antioxidants include vitamins C and E, beta-carotene (a form of vitamin A), selenium, lycopene, flavonoids, polyphenols, and more. These substances can be found naturally in foods such as fruits, vegetables, nuts, grains, some meats, poultry, and fish. Consuming antioxidant-rich foods may support overall health and potentially reduce risks associated with oxidative stress from free radicals. However, excessive intake through supplements might not offer additional benefits and could sometimes lead to adverse effects. Always consult healthcare providers before starting any new supplement regimen.

Anxiety is a feeling of unease, such as worry or fear, that can be mild or severe. It's a common human emotion often triggered by stressful situations but becomes a disorder when it's intense, excessive, and persistent, interfering with daily life. Types include generalized anxiety disorder, panic disorder, social anxiety disorder, etc. Symptoms may involve emotional and physical responses like restlessness, fatigue, difficulty concentrating, irritability, muscle tension, and sleep disturbances.

An Aortic Aneurysm is a bulge or weakening in the wall of the aorta, which is the main artery carrying blood from the heart to other parts of the body. This can occur anywhere along its length but most commonly happens in the abdominal section (abdominal aortic aneurysm - AAA) or just outside the heart (thoracic aortic aneurysm). If it grows too large, there's a risk that it could rupture, leading to severe internal bleeding, which is often fatal if not treated immediately. Regular screening for those at high risk, such as older men who have smoked, may help detect these before they become dangerous. Treatment options include monitoring small aneurysms with regular ultrasounds and surgical repair for larger ones.

Aphasia is an acquired communication disorder that impairs the ability to process language, affecting speaking, writing, gesturing, reading, and comprehension of spoken or written information. It typically results from brain damage caused by stroke, traumatic brain injury, or neurological conditions like dementia or tumors in areas responsible for speech and language function.

A1C (also known as hemoglobin A1c or HbA1c) is a blood test used to diagnose and monitor diabetes by measuring average blood glucose levels over the past 2-3 months.

Key points:
1. Measures glycated hemoglobin - hemoglobin bound with sugar in red blood cells.
2. Normal range for non-diabetic individuals typically falls below 5.7%.
3. For people diagnosed with diabetes, an ideal target often ranges from 6.5%-7%, but this can vary depending on individual circumstances.
4. The higher the percentage, generally indicates poorer control of blood sugars over time which may increase risk for complications related to diabetes such as heart disease, kidney damage etc.
5. Testing usually recommended twice yearly if well-controlled; more frequently otherwise.
6. Not affected by daily fluctuations in blood glucose like fingerstick tests, providing broader picture of long-term management effectiveness. 

Always consult healthcare provider regarding specific health concerns and testing needs.

It can vary from mild to severe and may result from various conditions affecting organs such as the stomach, intestines, liver, pancreas, kidneys, or reproductive system. Causes include gastritis, ulcers, irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), infections, appendicitis, kidney stones, among others. Severity and associated symptoms help determine its cause.

Induced abortions require medical supervision to ensure safety and minimize risks such as infection or hemorrhage. Laws governing abortion vary widely by country and region.

Symptoms often include pain, swelling, redness, and warmth at the site. Treatment usually involves antibiotics and sometimes drainage of the pus.

This nerve is responsible for transmitting sound and balance information from the ear to the brain. Symptoms can include hearing loss, tinnitus (ringing in the ears), dizziness, and imbalance. Treatment options vary depending on factors such as tumor size and patient health but may involve monitoring, surgery, or radiation therapy.

Acupuncture is an ancient form of Chinese medicine involving the insertion of thin needles into specific points (acupoints) in the body to balance energy flow or "Qi." It aims to treat various conditions by stimulating these acupoints believed to correlate with organs and bodily systems.

Research supports its use for pain relief, including chronic low back pain, neck pain, osteoarthritis, migraines, and headaches. Acupuncture may also help reduce nausea after surgery and chemotherapy treatments. However, evidence varies widely depending on the condition being treated.

The treatment is generally considered safe when performed by licensed practitioners using sterile equipment; common side effects include minor bruising at needle sites. Always consult healthcare providers before starting any new therapy regimen.

Symptoms typically resolve within two weeks without specific treatment beyond managing symptoms.

Acute lymphocytic leukemia (ALL), also known as acute lymphoblastic leukemia, is a fast-growing cancer that starts in the bone marrow and affects white blood cells called lymphocytes. In ALL, immature lymphocytes (lymphoblasts) multiply rapidly and crowd out normal blood-forming cells, leading to symptoms such as fatigue, frequent infections, and easy bruising or bleeding. Treatment often involves chemotherapy aimed at destroying these abnormal cells.

Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is a type of cancer that affects the blood and bone marrow. It progresses rapidly and involves the overproduction of abnormal white blood cells called blasts which do not function properly and interfere with normal blood cell production. This can lead to complications such as anemia, infections, and bleeding disorders. AML typically requires immediate treatment, often including chemotherapy or other targeted therapies depending on specific characteristics like genetic mutations present in the patient's leukemic cells.

Symptoms include fatigue, muscle weakness, weight loss, low blood pressure, and hyperpigmentation. Treatment typically involves hormone replacement therapy.

Adoption involves legal processes where an individual or couple assumes the parenting of a child whose birth parents cannot raise them for various reasons such as health issues, financial instability, or personal circumstances. Key aspects include:

1. **Types**: Domestic (within country) vs international; open (birth family has contact with adoptive family) vs closed adoptions.

2. **Legal Requirements**: Vary by jurisdiction but typically involve background checks, home studies, training sessions, and court proceedings to finalize the process legally.

3. **Rights & Responsibilities**: Adopted children have same rights as biological ones regarding inheritance, support from both sets of parents until adulthood, etc., while adoptive parents gain full parental responsibilities including guardianship over their adopted children's welfare decisions.

4. **Support Services**: Available pre-and post-adoption through agencies specializing in counseling services aimed at helping families navigate emotional challenges associated with this journey.

5. **Costs**: Can vary widely depending upon type chosen - domestic might cost less than $50k whereas some countries may charge up to several thousand dollars plus travel expenses if applicable.

Treatment often involves surgery to remove the tumor along with chemotherapy or radiation therapy for advanced cases. Prognosis varies widely but generally depends on whether the cancer has spread beyond the adrenal gland at diagnosis.

Adrenal gland disorders involve conditions that affect the function of the adrenal glands, which sit atop each kidney and produce hormones such as cortisol (for stress response) and aldosterone (to regulate blood pressure). Common types include:

1. **Addison's Disease**: A condition where the adrenal glands do not make enough steroid hormones due to damage or disease.

2. **Cushing’s Syndrome**: Characterized by excessive production of cortisol often caused by tumors in either the pituitary gland or elsewhere.

3. **Pheochromocytoma**: A tumor usually found within the medulla part of the adrenal gland leading to overproduction of catecholamines like adrenaline causing hypertension crises.

4. **Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia**: An inherited disorder affecting hormone synthesis primarily impacting children with severe imbalances from birth onwards.

Each disorder has specific symptoms related to hormonal imbalance requiring tailored treatment approaches including medication adjustments, surgery for some cases involving tumors, etc., under strict endocrinologist supervision.

Advanced directives are legal documents that allow individuals to communicate their wishes regarding healthcare treatments in situations where they may be unable to make decisions due to illness or incapacity. There are two main types:

1. **Living Will**: This document specifies what actions should be taken for your health if you are no longer able to make decisions yourself. It can outline preferences for life-sustaining treatment such as resuscitation, mechanical ventilation, dialysis, artificial nutrition (tube feeding), and hydration.

2. **Durable Power of Attorney for Healthcare (Healthcare Proxy)**: In this directive, an individual appoints another person (the proxy) to make healthcare decisions when they cannot do so themselves. The appointed person acts according to the expressed desires of the principal, which might also include instructions provided by a living will.

Both forms help ensure personal values guide care during incapacitating conditions while relieving family members from making difficult choices without clear guidance. These documents vary slightly depending on state laws within the U.S., thus it's important to consult local regulations or seek advice from a lawyer familiar with estate planning matters.
